newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council retains sanctions against Iraq.
newsitem.headline: UN Council retains sanctions against Iraq.

text.p: With Iraq and the United Nations embroiled in a controversy over missile parts, the Security Council on Tuesday retained blanket sanctions against Baghdad at its regular 60-day review.
The council had not been expected to alter the sanctions, imposed in August 1990 when Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait, especially in light of the recent conflict over the missiles.

A prime condition for an easing of the sanctions is a report to the council by the U.N. Special Commission that Iraq has fulfilled all obligations calling for the scrapping of its nuclear, chemical, biological and ballistic missile potential.

On Monday, the council censured Iraq for refusing to allow more than 100 missile engines to be taken abroad for examination by experts and reminded Baghdad of its obligation to comply with Gulf war disarmament resolutions.

Chief U.N. weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus said that he had again been unable to secure permission to remove Scud missile engines and other components which Iraq destroyed and buried without U.N. supervision soon after the 1991 Gulf war.

The council, however, has made an exception to the sanctions in the oil-for-food plan by allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months in order to buy necessities for its people, suffering under the embargoes. That programme went into effect on Dec. 10.

Council President Paulo Fulci of Italy told reporters that Ekeus's investigation into Iraq's missile capability "concerns not only the peace and security of the Gulf region but of the entire international community."
Iraq's failure to comply with council resolution would achieve "the indefinite prolongation of the present sanctions regime," he said.

Iraqi officials have said that they do not want the missile parts taken for analysis in the United States, where Ekeus intends on shipping them, but to another country, preferably Russia where they were originally manufactured.

U.S. representative Karl Inderfurth told the council that the missile controversy was a "watershed" event, one in which Iraq seeks to dictate to the agent of this council the terms and conditions of its cooperation with the Security Council."
